> A gold-backed-currency economy experiences inflation every time a new gold source is found for mining, even if new currency hasn't been minted yet.
This is not true. You are making a pure quantity theory argument while you ignore the quality theory of money. Simply increasing the money supply does not guarantee a rise in general prices, the Chinese experienced this after the warring states period.
After like 2 centuries of war and sending huge numbers of men to build parts of the Great Wall, china’s agricultural production has fallen significantly. The result was price inflation of food staples which the ruling government at the time attributed to a lack of money. So what did they do, they reduced the weight of copper in the money and minted more coinage of lesser quality. Prices inflated further. Eventually the abandoned the policy and returned to minting coinage with the proper weight of copper, they found prices stabilized regardless of how much new money they created. As long as the quality of the newly created money was consistent, prices did not inflate. This is quality theory of money.
In a commodity money standard, simply increasing the money supply will not result in a general rise in prices, especially when producing commodity money takes time. Now if you had a situation where suddenly out of no where, the amount of gold coinage in everyone’s pockets doubled, then yes there would be an acute price inflation. But that’s not and has never been a realistic scenario.

> The current global inflation situation (past 6 years) has as much or more to do with interruptions to the labor force and resources (oil) as anything else
Patently incorrect. The price inflation over the last few years is entirely the fault of the FED, who created 5 trillion in new dollars between 2020/2021 and injected these new dollars directly into the real economy via assets purchases from non-bank entities.
